name: Pectoralis major
func: The big fan-shaped chest muscle. It pulls the arm across the body, rotates it inward and helps push things away, like in a push-up or a bear hug.

levels.kid:
Put your hand flat on the front of your chest and squeeze your hands together. Feel that muscle get hard? That is your **pectoralis major**, or "pec" for short.

It is a big, flat muscle shaped like a **fan**. It starts at your middle chest and collarbone and joins onto your upper arm bone.

When you give someone a big **hug**, push a door open, do a push-up or throw a ball, your pec pulls your arm forward and across your body. You have one on each side of your chest.
levels.hs:
The **pectoralis major** is a large, fan-shaped muscle covering the upper front of the chest wall. It lies just under the skin and fat of the chest, on top of the smaller **pectoralis minor** and the ribs.

It has two main heads. The **clavicular head** starts on the inner half of the **clavicle**. The larger **sternocostal head** starts on the front of the **sternum** and the cartilages of the upper six ribs, with a small slip from the abdominal muscle sheath. The fibres converge into a flat, twisted tendon that inserts on the **lateral lip of the intertubercular (bicipital) groove** of the humerus.

Its lower border forms the **anterior axillary fold**, the front wall of the armpit.

Its main actions are **adduction** (pulling the arm toward the body) and **medial rotation** of the arm at the shoulder. The clavicular head also **flexes** the arm (raising it forward), while the sternocostal head **extends** a raised arm back down, as in climbing or swimming.

It is supplied by the **medial and lateral pectoral nerves**, branches of the brachial plexus. Next to it, the deltoid lies laterally, with the **deltopectoral groove** and cephalic vein in between.
levels.college:
**Attachments:** clavicular head from the anterior surface of the medial half of the clavicle; sternocostal head from the anterior sternum, costal cartilages 1–6 and the aponeurosis of the external oblique. Insertion: the lateral lip of the intertubercular groove of the humerus, beside latissimus dorsi (floor) and teres major (medial lip), giving the mnemonic "a lady between two majors".

**Tendon twist:** the tendon is bilaminar and folded. The clavicular fibres insert lowest and most anterior; the lowest sternocostal fibres twist behind to insert highest. This twist means the tendon is lengthened evenly when the arm is raised overhead.

**Innervation:** the **lateral pectoral nerve** (from the lateral cord, C5–C7) supplies mainly the clavicular head; the **medial pectoral nerve** (from the medial cord, C8–T1) pierces pectoralis minor and supplies the lower sternocostal part. This dual supply means the two heads can be tested separately for root level. Blood comes chiefly from the **pectoral branches of the thoraco-acromial artery**, plus perforators of the internal thoracic artery and the lateral thoracic artery.

**Relations:** deep to it are pectoralis minor and the **clavipectoral fascia**, pierced by the cephalic vein, thoraco-acromial artery and lateral pectoral nerve. The **axillary artery** and brachial plexus cords pass behind pectoralis minor, under cover of pectoralis major.

**Accessory action:** with the arm fixed, the pectoralis major can help lift the ribs in forced breathing.
levels.phd:
The pectoralis major is not one uniform muscle but a set of segments with distinct moment arms. Anatomical and MRI studies divide the sternocostal head into several sub-segments, each with its own nerve branch and fibre direction, and EMG shows the clavicular part activated preferentially in flexion and incline pressing while lower sternocostal parts dominate in arm depression. This **neuromuscular compartmentalisation** allows fine control of force direction.

Its moment arm changes dramatically with shoulder position. In abduction and external rotation, the long, lowest fibres are stretched near their limit, and eccentric loading in this position (the bench press at the bottom of the lift, or a tackle with the arm extended) places very high strain on the insertion, explaining the typical rupture site at the **musculotendinous junction or tendon insertion**.

Embryologically, the muscle derives from ventral limb-bud myoblasts that migrate from somites onto the chest wall. **Poland syndrome**, a congenital absence of the sternocostal head often with hand anomalies on the same side, is thought by many to result from interrupted blood flow in the **subclavian artery** during development (the subclavian artery supply disruption sequence), though the cause is not settled.

The muscle's reliable vascular pedicle makes it useful in reconstructive surgery: a **pectoralis major myocutaneous flap** based on the pectoral branch of the thoraco-acromial artery can be rotated up to cover defects in the neck, and a turnover flap based on internal thoracic perforators can cover the sternum after wound breakdown.
levels.expert:
**Exam:** test with resisted adduction from abduction ("press your palms together" or push the hand against the hip). Ask the patient to compare both **anterior axillary folds**; loss of the fold indicates rupture or absence.

**Pectoralis major rupture** typically occurs in weightlifters during the bench press. Signs: a pop, bruising spreading down the arm, asymmetry of the anterior axillary fold, a palpable defect and weakness in adduction and internal rotation. **MRI** confirms the site (insertion avulsion versus musculotendinous tear). Tendon avulsions in active people are usually repaired surgically, ideally early; muscle-belly tears are often managed without surgery.

**Poland syndrome** presents with absence of the sternocostal head, a flat chest wall on one side and sometimes short, webbed fingers on the same side.

**Root testing:** clavicular head weakness points to C5–C6; sternocostal head weakness points to C7–T1. In a C8–T1 root or medial cord lesion, the lower pec may be affected along with intrinsic hand muscles.

The deltopectoral interval is the standard **surgical approach** to the shoulder for fracture fixation and joint replacement. The cephalic vein is identified and usually retracted laterally with the deltoid.

The pectoralis major myocutaneous flap remains a workhorse in **head and neck reconstruction**. In neonates, **pectoral muscle absence** on a chest X-ray can appear as a hyperlucent hemithorax, a subtle sign that should not be mistaken for lung disease.

keyPoints: Fan-shaped chest muscle with clavicular and sternocostal heads
Inserts on the lateral lip of the intertubercular groove
Adducts and medially rotates the arm
Ruptures in bench pressing; Poland syndrome = congenital absence

test.q: What are the main actions of pectoralis major at the shoulder?
test.explain: It pulls the arm toward and across the body and rotates it inward.

test.q: The lower border of pectoralis major forms the anterior ______ fold.
test.explain: Loss of this fold is a key sign of rupture.

choices: Medial lip of the intertubercular groove
Lateral lip of the intertubercular groove
test.explain: 'A lady between two majors': latissimus dorsi in the floor, teres major medial, pec major lateral.

test.q: Which activity classically causes a pectoralis major tendon rupture?
test.explain: Eccentric load with the arm abducted and externally rotated strains the insertion.

test.q: Congenital absence of the sternocostal head of pectoralis major is called ______ syndrome.
test.explain: It may come with hand anomalies on the same side.
